Tesla’s net income attributable to common stockholders fell from **$14,997 million in FY2023** to **$7,091 million in FY2024** and **$3,794 million in FY2025**—derived declines of **52.7%** and **46.5%**, respectively, or **74.7% cumulatively** over the three years. [S4][S8][S12] The comparison is materially affected by the release of a U.S. deferred-tax valuation allowance in fourth-quarter 2023, while automotive margin pressure and unfavorable bitcoin and foreign-exchange movements also affected subsequent earnings. [S36][S23][S18][S35]

## Tesla: three-year net income trend

| Fiscal year / period | Net income attributable to common stockholders | Year-over-year change |
|---|---:|---:|
| FY2023: 12 months ended December 31, 2023 | $14,997 million [S4] | — |
| FY2024: 12 months ended December 31, 2024 | $7,091 million [S8] | **−52.7%**, derived [S8][S4] |
| FY2025: 12 months ended December 31, 2025 | $3,794 million [S12] | **−46.5%**, derived [S12][S8] |

### What drove the change?

- **FY2023 was boosted by a tax benefit.** Read from the Filing text, Tesla reported a **$5,001 million income-tax benefit** for FY2023; its deferred-tax valuation allowance decreased by **$6.46 billion**, primarily due to releasing the allowance on U.S. federal and certain state deferred-tax assets. [S25] This makes FY2023 an unusually favorable earnings comparison rather than a clean operating baseline. [S25][S36]

- **FY2024’s decline reflected the tax comparison and automotive pressure.** Tesla stated that its provision for income taxes “changed by $6.84 billion,” with its effective tax rate moving from a **50% benefit to a 20% expense**, primarily because of the fourth-quarter 2023 allowance release; these figures are read from the Filing text. [S36] In Q2 FY2024, automotive gross margin fell from **19.2% to 18.5%**, driven by lower vehicle average selling prices and temporary manufacturing under-utilization during production ramps, partly offset by regulatory-credit revenue and lower vehicle costs. [S17] There was a partial recovery in Q3: net income rose **16.9% year over year, derived**, to **$2,167 million** for the three months ended September 30, 2024. [S7][S3]

- **FY2025 brought further earnings deterioration.** Automotive gross margin fell from **19.0% to 16.9%** for the nine months ended September 30, reflecting automotive revenue and cost changes and lower regulatory-credit revenue. [S18] For the full year, Tesla said other income/expense “changed unfavorably by $1.11 billion,” primarily from bitcoin mark-to-market movements and foreign-exchange fluctuations on intercompany balances. [S35] Its effective tax rate also increased from **20% to 27%**, reflecting jurisdictional earnings mix and OBBBA-related tax effects; these annual figures are read from the Filing text. [S35]

### Coverage

No Coverage Gaps were listed. Annual figures use Tesla’s **10-K FY2023, report period 2023-12-31; 10-K FY2024, report period 2024-12-31; and 10-K FY2025, report period 2025-12-31**. [S4][S8][S12] Quarterly context uses **10-Q Q2 FY2024 (2024-06-30), Q3 FY2024 (2024-09-30), and Q3 FY2025 (2025-09-30)**. [S17][S7][S18] The excerpts do not provide a complete quantified bridge attributing each year’s net-income decline to individual drivers.
items.fact: Tesla's net income attributable to common stockholders was $3.79 billion in 2025.

[S1] [S5] [S2] [S6] [S3] [S7] Q4 FY2024 revenue was **$48,386 million**, derived from FY2024 revenue less Q1–Q3; Q4 FY2025 was **$59,894 million**, derived the same way from FY2025 revenue. The Q4 year-over-year increase of 23.8% is also derived from those quarterly figures. [S4] [S1] [S2] [S3] [S8] [S5] [S6] [S7]

### What drove the change

Meta’s FY2025 filing text says advertising revenue increased **$35.54 billion, or 22%**, due to increases in ad impressions and average price per ad. Impressions rose 12% and average price per ad rose 9% year over year; Meta linked the latter to increased advertising demand, which it believes is mostly due to ongoing improvements to ad targeting and measurement tools. Impressions grew in all regions, especially Asia-Pacific, driven by increases in users and engagement. [S14]

Family of Apps (FoA) revenue increased **$36.40 billion, or 22%**, while Reality Labs (RL) revenue increased **$61 million, or 3%**. FoA’s increase was almost entirely driven by advertising; its other revenue rose $862 million, or 50%, mostly from WhatsApp paid messaging and Meta Verified subscriptions. RL’s modest increase reflected higher AI-glasses sales, partly offset by lower Meta Quest sales. [S14]

**Coverage:** No Coverage Gaps are listed. The filings cover FY2024 and FY2025, but do not provide revenue after FY2025.

## Bank of America — disclosure timeline

| Filing | Report period | Risk-factor disclosure |
|---|---|---|
| Form 10-K, FY2024 | 2024-12-31 | Provides the substantive risk-factor baseline. [S1] |

### Material issues in the unchanged baseline

These are **existing disclosures, not newly added 2025 risks**. [S1][S2][S3][S4]

- **Interest rates, securities and funding:** Higher rates generally benefited net interest income but negatively affected investment securities, deposits, loan demand and funding costs. Lower rates would typically reduce revenue through lower net interest income. Rising rates or wider spreads could reduce debt-security values, impair liquidity and, for available-for-sale securities, adversely affect accumulated other comprehensive income and capital. [S1]
- **Capital requirements and distributions:** The FY2024 filing text states that the stress capital buffer increased by **70 bps to 3.2 percent** in 2024 and the G-SIB surcharge increased **50 bps to 3.0 percent**. - **Specific compliance remediation:** In **December 2024**, the OCC issued a Consent Order against BANA concerning aspects of its Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money laundering and economic sanctions compliance programs. - **Credit deterioration:** Commercial real estate, “particularly office,” remained exposed to shifts in demand and tight financial and credit conditions. Inflation, higher household debt and elevated debt-servicing costs could weaken borrower performance; insufficient expected-credit-loss estimates could require provisions that reduce earnings. [S1]
- **Cybersecurity and emerging technology:** The bank identified ransomware, phishing, vishing and smishing, third-party vulnerabilities, and AI-enabled threats. It reported no material losses or other material consequences from cybersecurity incidents, information breaches or technology failures, while expecting such events and impacts with increased frequency and severity. [S1]

On the filings' own language, **JPMorgan Chase** has the broadest and most structural regulatory exposure. It describes its businesses as "highly regulated and... significantly affected by applicable law and supervisory expectations," with regulation reaching its capital, distributions and operations [S4]. Apple and Tesla also face heavy, specific regulation: Apple through the EU Digital Markets Act and a U.S. App Store court order [S1], and Tesla through autonomy, EV-incentive and direct-sales rules [S3]. For them, though, regulation is one risk among many rather than a constraint on how the whole business runs. This ranking is a qualitative reading; none of the filings ranks itself against the others. The filings also cover different periods, so this is not a same-period comparison.

## JPMorgan Chase (10-K FY2025, report period 2025-12-31)
- **Supervision shapes the business.** JPM says it is subject to "extensive supervision and regulation that significantly affects the way that it conducts its business and structures its operations." It has in the past modified its business in response, for example by limiting products, raising prices, reducing market-making liquidity, paying higher taxes or disposing of assets [S4].
- **Capital rules limit shareholder returns.** Required capital can rise from actions by banking regulators, from changes that increase RWA, or from Federal Reserve CCAR stress losses that increase its SCB [S4]. A shortfall could reduce buybacks, constrain dividends and curtail business activities [S4].
- **Enforcement history.** JPM "has in the past incurred significant penalties." Governmental authorities have required admissions of wrongdoing, and officials have increasingly required institutions to plead guilty to criminal offenses [S4].
- **Uneven rules across competitors.** Larger firms "often face more stringent supervision," while fintech competitors may not be subject to banking regulation [S4].
- **Other regulatory exposures.** These include standards for overseeing vendors, evolving AI law, and resolution, under which security holders would absorb losses [S4].

## Apple (10-K FY2025, report period 2025-09-27; 10-Q Q1 FY2026, report period 2025-12-27)
- **Breadth of laws.** Apple lists laws spanning antitrust, privacy, data localization, online safety, age verification, AI, tax, trade and e-waste, among others. It calls compliance "onerous and expensive" [S1].
- **EU Digital Markets Act.** Apple changed iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari in the EU, including alternative fee structures, distribution and payment processing. Its compliance plan "has been challenged by the Commission," and the DMA provides for significant fines [S1].
- **U.S. App Store.** Apple is subject to a court order "preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases" [S1].
- **Trade.** Regulatory changes may come "with little or no advance notice," and Apple's products "could be banned, delayed or prohibited from importation" [S1].
- **No update since the 10-K.** The Q1 FY2026 10-Q reports no material changes to these risk factors [S2].

## Tesla (10-K FY2025, report period 2025-12-31)
- **Autonomy and the Robotaxi service.** Tesla launched autonomous ride-hailing in 2025. It warns of a "patchwork of complex or conflicting regulations," including standards "drafted assuming the presence of a human driver." NHTSA's Standing General Order requires reports on certain crashes involving these systems [S3].
- **Incentives.** Recent actions "have repealed and/or restricted consumer, manufacturing and charging infrastructure tax credits," along with certain regulatory credit programs. The OBBBA requires traceability of critical minerals to keep products eligible for credits [S3].
- **Direct sales.** State dealer-franchise laws may limit Tesla's stores and dealer licenses [S3].
- **Other regulation.** Tesla cites environmental and safety laws in the U.S., China and Germany, GDPR, the CCPA, and net-metering reforms contested before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission [S3]. It also notes possible action by the SEC or the U.S. Department of Justice [S3].

## Coverage
- **Coverage gap: periods differ.** The Companies' latest Filings here cover different periods (Apple: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-09-27; Tesla: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31; JPMorgan Chase: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31), so the comparison is not of the same period.
- **No quantified measure.** The Sources contain no figures for compliance costs, fines paid or capital requirements, so regulatory exposure cannot be compared in dollar terms. The ranking above rests only on the qualitative risk-factor text.
items.fact: Tesla says the EU's General Data Protection Regulation carries a significant risk of fines for noncompliance.

items.answer:
JPMorgan Chase appears to have the broadest and most directly embedded regulatory exposure in these filings: it describes extensive supervision and regulation affecting how it conducts business and structures operations, as well as possible restrictions on products, pricing, market-making, assets and business activities. The filings do not provide a common measure that would establish which company has the greatest exposure quantitatively, and their reporting periods differ. [S4]

### Apple

- Apple’s FY2025 10-K, for the year ended September 27, 2025, describes worldwide legal and regulatory exposure spanning antitrust, privacy, data security and localization, online safety and age verification, digital platforms, AI, labor, trade, tax and environmental rules; it says compliance is onerous and expensive and may increase costs or require changes to products, services or supply chains. [S1]
- The filing gives concrete examples of business changes: Apple implemented changes to developer communications about alternative purchasing mechanisms in the U.S. App Store and is subject to a court order preventing certain commissions or fees; in the EU it changed iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari to address the Digital Markets Act, including alternative distribution, payment processing and fee structures, and says its compliance plan has been challenged by the Commission. [S1]
- Apple’s Q1 FY2026 10-Q, for the quarter ended December 27, 2025, reports no material changes to the FY2025 10-K risk factors. [S2]

### Tesla

- Tesla’s FY2025 10-K, for the year ended December 31, 2025, identifies regulation across environmental, occupational, health and safety requirements; vehicle safety, fuel economy and emissions; privacy; direct vehicle sales; and energy-system imports, grid interconnection and electricity sales. [S3]
- Its filing identifies specific exposure to changing incentives: recent governmental and regulatory actions repealed or restricted consumer, manufacturing and charging-infrastructure tax credits and certain regulatory credit programs, while OBBBA provisions could affect battery-cell expenses and consumer costs; insufficient critical-mineral origin documentation could also cost products eligibility for tax credits and incentives. [S3]
- Tesla also says changing rules for driver-assistance features and autonomous capability may restrict designs or functionality or slow its Robotaxi expansion, and differing foreign vehicle standards can require additional investment and regulatory review before market entry. [S3]

### JPMorgan Chase

- JPMorgan Chase’s FY2025 10-K, for the year ended December 31, 2025, presents supervision and regulation as a central exposure: changing law, interpretations, supervisory expectations or executive actions could require business modifications, raise costs or reduce revenues, while noncompliance could bring scrutiny, enforcement, penalties, litigation or reputational harm. [S4]
- It specifically warns that regulators could require it to limit products, raise prices, reduce market-making liquidity, pay higher taxes or charges, dispose of assets, forgo opportunities or otherwise restrict activities; larger firms may face more stringent oversight, while less-regulated competitors and differences in international implementation may put it at a disadvantage. [S4]
- The filing also describes recurring examinations and potentially overlapping proceedings across U.S. and non-U.S. authorities, with past penalties and remediation costs, and says capital requirements can restrict buybacks, dividends, executive bonuses or business activity. [S4]

**Coverage:** Periods differ: Apple’s latest filing here is its 10-K FY2025, year ended September 27, 2025; Tesla’s and JPMorgan Chase’s are 10-K FY2025 filings, each for the year ended December 31, 2025. [S1][S3][S4] The Sources do not quantify comparable regulatory exposure or establish a definitive measured ranking; Apple’s Q1 FY2026 10-Q provides no material risk-factor changes. [S2]

Tesla’s 2026 outlook centers on a substantial increase in investment in AI, autonomy, robotics and manufacturing: its MD&A says capital expenditures are expected to be “in excess of $20 billion in 2026.” [S1] **No guidance in the Filings: Tesla's own guidance is not in the Filings provided; the outlook below is drawn from MD&A commentary and risk factors.** The key financial tension is that Tesla says heightened capital expenditures will necessitate additional funding beyond operating cash flow, although it considers its liquidity adequate. [S1]

## Tesla — 2026 investment and operating priorities

**AI infrastructure and production ramps.** The FY2025 Form 10-K, report period December 31, 2025, attributes the expected spending to compute infrastructure and data centers; manufacturing and R&D production lines and facilities; company-operated AI-enabled assets; and its retail, service and charging footprint. [S1] For context, actual 2025 capital expenditures were **$8.53 billion**, read from the Filing text. [S1]

Tesla says it will ramp **six new production lines across vehicle, Bots, energy storage and battery manufacturing in 2026**. [S18] It is building **Cortex 2 at Gigafactory Texas** to increase AI training compute capacity, following the expansion of Cortex in 2025 and an announced collaboration with Samsung to manufacture advanced AI inference and training semiconductors in the U.S. [S18]

**Automotive and autonomy.** Tesla describes the next phase of production growth as driven by advances in autonomy, new products—including those using its next-generation vehicle platform—and its ability to manufacture proprietary cells at high volume, with lower capital and production costs and longer range. [S1] It also says it has continued expanding and refining Robotaxi following its **June 2025 launch**, seeking to advance a service-driven business model. [S1] The excerpts do not quantify 2026 vehicle deliveries, revenue, earnings or Robotaxi economics.

**Energy storage and supply-chain integration.** Tesla is focused on ramping production and market penetration of energy storage products after deploying **46.7 GWh in 2025**. [S1] Its MD&A identifies rapid electricity-load growth from AI infrastructure as an opportunity for storage to stabilize the grid, shift energy and provide additional power capacity. [S1] Its in-house Texas lithium refinery began operations in **January 2026**, supporting regional supply-chain localization and vertical integration. [S18]

## Funding capacity and execution risks

Tesla ended 2025 with **$44.06 billion in cash, cash equivalents and investments** and generated **$14.75 billion of operating cash flow in 2025**, both read from the Filing text. [S1] It generally expects positive operating cash flow, but may raise capital, use debt facilities or slow spending if manufacturing ramps more slowly than expected. [S1] Separately, on **January 16, 2026**, it agreed to invest approximately **$2 billion in xAI Series E Preferred Stock**, subject to limited closing conditions, including regulatory approvals. [S2]

Trade-policy changes could alter project timelines and capital spending; rising material, supply-chain and labor costs could increase funding needs. [S1] Tesla is also evaluating the OBBBA’s 2026 effects, including loss of certain regulatory-credit sales and changes to product costs. [S4]

**Coverage:** Uses Tesla’s **10-K FY2025, report period 2025-12-31**. [S1][S2][S4][S18] No guidance in the Filings: Tesla's own guidance is not in the Filings provided; the outlook above is drawn from MD&A commentary and risk factors. The excerpts do not provide quantified 2026 revenue, earnings, delivery or margin targets.

UnitedHealth's latest annual report, the FY2024 10-K (report period 2024-12-31), says its cybersecurity exposure comes from the large volume of protected personal data it handles, a history of actual compromises, and threat actors who increasingly use AI. It names a 2024 cyberattack on Change Healthcare as a concrete example [S1]. The 10-Qs for Q1 through Q3 FY2025 state that there have been "no material changes to the risk factors as disclosed in our 2024 10-K" [S2][S3][S4].

## UnitedHealth Group Inc (UNH)

Source: 10-K, FY2024, report period 2024-12-31 (Risk Factors, Item 1A) [S1]. The following points come from that filing unless otherwise noted.

**Data exposure and prior incidents**
- The company "routinely process[es], store[s] and transmit[s] large amounts of data," including "protected personal information subject to privacy, security or data breach notification laws," and some of this data may be outside the United States [S1].
- It is "regularly the target of attempted cyberattacks" and "have previously been, and may in the future be, subject to compromises" of its systems and of information held by third parties [S1].
- It "previously reported our Change Healthcare business, which we had recently acquired, was subject to a cyberattack in 2024, in which the data involved contained protected health information or personally identifiable information" [S1].

**Threat techniques**
- Techniques "are increasing in sophistication, in part due to use of evolving AI/ML technologies (including generative AI)," so the company "may be unable to anticipate these techniques and threats, timely detect data security incidents or implement adequate preventive measures" [S1].
- The filing names ransomware and malware, noting threat actors can "exploit any security vulnerabilities, and disrupt or shutdown our systems and operations" [S1].
- It also cites "financial fraud schemes, misplaced or lost data, error, malicious social engineering" as vulnerabilities [S1].
- Software defects are a separate risk: hardware, software or applications "may contain defects or other problems which could unexpectedly compromise our information security controls" [S1].

**Acquired and third-party exposure**
- "There have previously been and may be in the future heightened vulnerabilities due to recently-acquired or non-integrated businesses" [S1].
- Third-party vendors process and store large amounts of its data, and their operations "are outside our direct oversight and control" [S1].

**Consequences the filing lists**
- Costs to address security threats "could be material," and remediation failures could cause "operational interruptions, delays, or cessation of service and loss of existing or potential customers" [S1].
- Compromises could expose people to "financial or medical identity theft," lead to "litigation and liability, including regulatory penalties," and damage the brand and reputation [S1].
- The filing also says that failing to comply with privacy, security and data laws could bring "significant fines, penalties and litigation awards" [S1].

**Related AI/ML risk**
- The company says inadequate compliance with its responsible AI/ML policies, or with "emerging laws, regulations and standards governing AI/ML use," could cause technology products "not to operate as intended" and lead to "possible regulatory enforcement action or litigation" [S1].

## Coverage

- **Coverage Gaps:** None.
- **Sources used:** UNH 10-K FY2024 (report period 2024-12-31) [S1]; the 10-Q for Q1, Q2 and Q3 FY2025 risk-factor sections, which only confirm no material changes from the 2024 10-K [S2][S3][S4].
- **Not answered by the Sources:** The excerpts do not give the financial cost of the Change Healthcare incident, the number of people affected, or any insurance recovery. They also do not describe the company's specific security controls beyond the general programs mentioned in the filing, and they do not report any 2025 cyber incidents, since the 10-Qs state no risk-factor changes.
items.fact: UnitedHealth identified on February 21, 2024 that cybercrime threat actors had gained access to certain Change Healthcare systems.

Apple, Tesla and JPMorgan Chase each identify risks that could materially harm their businesses, but their exposures differ: Apple highlights global product demand, supply-chain concentration, tariffs and technology-market regulation; Tesla emphasizes executing product and manufacturing ramps, supplier availability, vehicle and energy-product risks, and its dependence on key personnel; JPMorgan’s risk profile centers on financial regulation, market and credit conditions, liquidity and capital requirements, and operational and cyber resilience. [S1] [S3] [S4] These filings cover different periods—Apple’s 10-K for FY2025, year ended 2025-09-27, and Tesla’s and JPMorgan Chase’s 10-Ks for FY2025, each year ended 2025-12-31—so this is not a same-period comparison. [S1] [S3] [S4]

### Apple

Apple identifies dependence on global and regional economic conditions as a material risk: slow growth or recession, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates and currency fluctuations can weaken consumer confidence and spending. [S1] Its international sales represent a majority of net sales, and a majority of supplier facilities—including manufacturing and assembly sites—are outside the U.S., increasing exposure to disruption across its global supply chain. [S1]

Trade measures are a specific current concern: beginning in Q2 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced, including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU; other countries imposed or threatened reciprocal tariffs. [S1] Apple also points to the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Section 232 investigation into imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and derivative products containing semiconductors; the eventual impact remains uncertain. [S1]

Operationally, Apple relies on outsourcing partners, primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, and partners in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware products; it also relies on single-source suppliers for components. [S1] The company cites risks from shortages and price increases, defects, product-transition execution and demand forecasting. [S1] Regulatory exposure includes EU Digital Markets Act changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari, as well as U.S. changes to developer communications and a court order concerning commissions or fees on certain purchases. [S1] Apple’s Q1 FY2026 10-Q says there were no material changes to its risk factors since the FY2025 10-K. [S2]

### Tesla

Tesla’s central execution risk is developing, launching and ramping products and services on time and at planned cost, quality and output. Its filing specifically names driver assistance and autonomous driving, mass-market vehicles including Cybercab, Bots including Optimus, energy storage products and Solar Roof. [S3] It says future success depends on advancing AI capabilities, building efficient manufacturing and supply chains, and hiring and training skilled employees. [S3]

Tesla also faces supply risks from thousands of globally purchased parts and hundreds of suppliers, including single-source direct suppliers. It says 2025 U.S. trade-policy changes, including heightened import tariffs and retaliatory measures, have affected supply-chain costs and may affect component availability. [S3] Further exposures include lithium-ion cell production and safety, product liability, and self-insurance for vehicle product-liability exposure in most jurisdictions. [S3] The filing also identifies dependence on CEO Elon Musk and the challenge of attracting and retaining qualified personnel. [S3]

### JPMorgan Chase

JPMorgan’s filing foregrounds extensive supervision and regulation: legal or supervisory changes can require it to limit products, raise prices, reduce market-making liquidity, pay higher taxes, dispose of assets or forgo opportunities; noncompliance can bring enforcement actions, penalties, litigation or reputational harm. [S4] Its consumer business is exposed to unemployment, inflation, interest-rate changes, housing and vehicle collateral values, and consumer debt, which can raise delinquencies, credit-loss allowances and net charge-offs. [S4]

Other material exposures include constrained liquidity, credit-rating downgrades that raise funding costs or trigger collateral requirements, and regulatory capital requirements that can limit dividends, share repurchases or business activity. [S4] Operationally, JPMorgan reports past system disruptions affecting customers, including inability to access accounts, exfiltration of personal data and duplicative transactions; it says future cyber breaches are inevitable and could cause losses, investigations, penalties and reputational harm. [S4]

### Coverage

Coverage gap: **Periods differ**: the Companies’ latest Filings here cover different periods (Apple: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-09-27; Tesla: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31; JPMorgan Chase: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31), so the comparison is not of the same period. The sources describe risk factors, not their likelihood, relative financial magnitude or a common quantitative ranking.

- **FY2024 — 10-K, FY2024, Report Period 2024-01-28:** Revenue was **$60,922 million for the 12 months ended 2024-01-28**. The 10-K said FY2024 revenue was up **126%** year over year, driven by Data Center revenue growth of **217%**. It cited demand across enterprise software, consumer internet, and automotive, financial-services, and healthcare verticals. [S4] [S19]  
  The commentary looked toward ongoing demand for AI infrastructure: in Q4 FY2024, large cloud providers represented more than half of Data Center revenue, and NVIDIA estimated approximately 40% of FY2024 Data Center revenue was for AI inference. [S19]

- **FY2025 — 10-K, FY2025, Report Period 2025-01-26:** Revenue was **$130,497 million for the 12 months ended 2025-01-26**, up **114%** year over year. NVIDIA attributed the increase primarily to demand for its Hopper accelerated-computing platform; it also said it began shipping production systems of the Blackwell architecture in Q4 FY2025. Data Center revenue was up **142%** year over year. [S8] [S18]  
  The earlier 10-Q commentary had been more explicitly prospective: the Q2 FY2025 10-Q said Blackwell production was scheduled to begin in Q4 and continue into FY2026, and said NVIDIA expected to ship “several billion dollars” of Blackwell revenue in Q4 FY2025. UnitedHealth’s latest annual report identifies cybersecurity risks from attacks on its own systems and third-party vendors, and from failures to protect sensitive information or maintain reliable operations. The 2024 Form 10-K describes a 2024 cyberattack on its recently acquired Change Healthcare business involving protected health information or personally identifiable information; the Q3 FY2025 Form 10-Q says there were no material changes to the risk factors disclosed in that annual report. [S1][S2]

## Cybersecurity risks described

The 10-K says UnitedHealth routinely processes, stores and transmits large amounts of data, including protected personal information covered by privacy, security and breach-notification laws, as well as proprietary or confidential information. Some data may be outside the United States because of its information systems and international operations. The company says it is regularly targeted by attempted cyberattacks and has previously experienced compromises of its systems or information, including the Change Healthcare incident. [S1]

The filing describes several ways an incident could occur: threat actors may penetrate security controls, disrupt or shut down systems and operations, or access, misappropriate or otherwise compromise protected personal information and confidential or proprietary information. They may also deploy viruses, ransomware or other malware, exploit security vulnerabilities, or use financial fraud schemes, misplaced or lost data, error, or malicious social engineering. The company warns that attack techniques change frequently and are becoming more sophisticated, including through evolving AI/ML technologies such as generative AI, making them difficult to anticipate or detect promptly. [S1]

Risks extend beyond UnitedHealth’s own systems. The company relies on third-party vendors to process, store and transmit substantial amounts of business data, and says those vendors face similar risks outside its direct oversight and control. Hardware, software or applications developed or procured from third parties may contain defects or other problems that unexpectedly compromise information-security controls. Recently acquired or non-integrated businesses may also have heightened vulnerabilities. [S1]

Potential consequences named in the 10-K include operational interruptions, delays or cessation of service; lost existing or potential customers; increased costs to address security threats or remediate incidents; and negative operational effects. A compromise or unauthorized disclosure could also expose UnitedHealth or others to financial or medical identity theft, litigation and liability, including regulatory penalties, reputational or brand damage, and loss or misuse of information. The filing notes that these events could harm revenue and the company’s business, results of operations, financial position and cash flows. [S1]

UnitedHealth says it has programs to detect, contain and respond to incidents, employee awareness training on phishing, malware and other cyber threats, and business-continuity and resiliency plans that it maintains, updates and tests regularly. It nevertheless expects to continue experiencing incidents, some of which may negatively affect the business, and cautions that remediation may not succeed. [S1]

## Coverage

The annual-report discussion is from UNH’s 10-K for FY2024, report period December 31, 2024; the latest update is its Q3 FY2025 10-Q, report period September 30, 2025, which reports no material risk-factor changes. [S1][S2] Coverage Gaps: None. The excerpts do not quantify the likelihood or potential financial impact of future cybersecurity incidents.
items.fact: UnitedHealth identified on February 21, 2024 that cybercrime threat actors had gained access to certain Change Healthcare systems.

Merck's FY2024 10-K describes regulatory risk centered on U.S. drug-pricing law. Under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), Januvia, Janumet and Janumet XR face government-set prices, and Merck expects Keytruda to be selected in 2026, with U.S. Keytruda sales declining after its set price takes effect on January 1, 2028 [S1]. Bristol Myers Squibb is not in the filings provided, so this answer does not cover it.

## Merck & Co Inc (MRK): 10-K, FY2024, report period 2024-12-31

**U.S. drug-pricing legislation**
- **IRA (2022):** Merck says the law makes significant changes to how drugs are covered and paid for under Medicare [S1]. These include:
  - financial penalties for drugs whose prices rise faster than inflation;
  - a Medicare Part D redesign that took effect in 2025 and makes manufacturers bear more of the benefit liability;
  - government price setting for Part D drugs starting in 2026 and Part B drugs starting in 2028 [S1].
- **Products affected by IRA price setting** [S1]:
  - Januvia: set price effective January 1, 2026.
  - Janumet and Janumet XR: selected January 17, 2025, with prices effective January 1, 2027.
  - Keytruda: expected to be selected in 2026, with a price effective January 1, 2028.
- **Why Keytruda matters:** Keytruda was 46% of Merck's 2024 total sales [S1]. Merck also warns that government price setting may affect pricing in the private market [S1].
- **American Rescue Plan Act (2021):** It removed the cap on Medicaid rebates, previously 100% of Average Manufacturer Price (AMP), starting January 2024. Merck may now pay state Medicaid programs more in rebates than it received on sales of some products [S1].
- **340B and state action:**
  - Greater use of the 340B Federal Drug Discount Program is hurting performance [S1].
  - Merck expects states to use Prescription Drug Affordability Boards with authority to set upper payment limits [S1].

**FDA, HHS and vaccine policy**
- Merck says HHS could change in ways that make it harder for the FDA to approve drugs and vaccines, and for the CDC to issue or maintain vaccine recommendations [S1].
- If FDA user fee programs were eliminated, facility inspections and approvals could be significantly delayed [S1].
- Biologics and vaccines face more complex regulation. For example, FDA approval is generally required to release each commercial human vaccine lot [S1].
- After approval, risks include post-approval Phase 4 results and withdrawal of indications granted under accelerated approval [S1]. Merck also notes greater safety focus by the FDA, EMA, Japan's PMDA and China's NMPA [S1].

**International, compliance and trade**
- **China:** A government anti-corruption campaign with more inspections and audits could hurt sales [S1].
- **Laws and regulations Merck lists** [S1]:
  - the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA);
  - data privacy rules in the EU, U.S. and China;
  - mandates for local manufacturing;
  - the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the SEC's climate rules (currently stayed) and California's greenhouse gas (GHG) reporting law.
- **Compulsory licensing:** Some foreign governments may grant compulsory licenses to Merck's patents [S1].
- **Tariffs:** The U.S. plans tariff increases, particularly on Canada and Mexico, and has already raised tariffs on China [S1].

**Tax**
- The IRS is examining Merck's 2017–2018 returns, including the one-time transition tax under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). An adverse finding could create a significant tax liability [S1].
- The IRS is also examining Merck's 2021–2022 returns [S1].
- Other tax risks include the OECD two-pillar reform and the tax-free status of the 2021 Organon spin-off [S1].

## Coverage
- **Coverage gap:** Bristol Myers Squibb is not in the filings provided, so this answer does not cover it. No comparison between the two companies is possible.
- **Merck's filings:** Merck is a snapshot company with one filing, the 10-K for FY2024 (report period 2024-12-31). Trends over time cannot be assessed.
- **What the sources do not answer:** They give no dollar estimates of the IRA's impact on Januvia, Janumet or Keytruda, and they contain no company guidance. The statements above are risk-factor disclosures.

Apple, Tesla and JPMorgan Chase face different core exposures: Apple’s filing emphasizes product demand, global supply-chain and trade disruption, and legal and regulatory changes; Tesla highlights execution of new products and production ramps, supplier and manufacturing risks, and vehicle, technology and financing exposures; JPMorgan’s risk summary is centered on legal and regulatory, market and credit, liquidity and capital, and operational risks. [S1][S3][S4] The comparison uses Apple’s 10-K for FY2025, report period 2025-09-27, and Tesla’s and JPMorgan Chase’s 10-Ks for FY2025, report period 2025-12-31; **periods differ**, so this is not a same-period comparison. [S1][S3][S4]

### Apple

- **Demand, margins and supply chain:** Apple says results depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions, which can affect consumer confidence and spending. It identifies pricing pressure, competition, product mix, component and manufacturing costs, foreign exchange and tariffs as factors that can increase volatility or pressure net sales and gross margins. [S1]
- **Trade and production concentration:** A significant majority of manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam; Apple also relies on single-source partners for many components and partners primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware products. The filing cites U.S. tariffs announced beginning in Q2 2025, including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, and says the ultimate impact remains uncertain. [S1]
- **Regulatory and product risks:** Apple identifies legal proceedings and government investigations, including competition-related requirements and the EU Digital Markets Act. It has changed iOS, iPadOS, the App Store and Safari in the EU, including alternative distribution and payment processing; the Commission has challenged its compliance plan, and the DMA provides for significant fines and penalties. Apple also warns that product or software defects, including in complex AI features, could lead to safety, security, warranty, liability and reputational costs. [S1]

### Tesla

- **Execution and scaling:** Tesla says it may face delays in developing, launching and ramping products, services and features, or fail to control manufacturing costs. It specifically points to driver-assistance and autonomous-driving development, Cybercab, Bots including Optimus, and the need to scale AI capabilities, facilities, supply chains and skilled staffing. [S3]
- **Suppliers, manufacturing and trade:** Tesla’s products contain thousands of parts sourced globally from hundreds of suppliers, including single-source suppliers. Its filing says 2025 U.S. trade-policy alterations, including heightened import tariffs and subsequent retaliatory measures, have impacted supply-chain costs and may affect component availability. It also identifies lithium-ion cell production and Gigafactory operations as important to vehicle and energy-storage production and profitability. [S3]
- **Product, financing and people exposure:** Tesla warns that battery-cell failures could cause fires and disrupt operations, and says it generally self-insures vehicle product-liability exposure in most jurisdictions. Financing programs expose it to residual-value, funding and customer-credit risks; the filing also says Tesla is highly dependent on CEO Elon Musk and may have difficulty attracting and retaining qualified personnel. [S3]

### JPMorgan Chase

- **Regulation and markets:** JPMorgan says extensive supervision and regulation can require it to limit products, raise prices, reduce market-making liquidity, dispose of assets or forgo opportunities, increasing costs or reducing revenues. Its market risks include changes in rates and credit spreads, political and economic events, declines in asset values and difficulty hedging positions. [S4]
- **Credit, liquidity and capital:** Its filing highlights borrower, counterparty and collateral risks; consumer stress could increase delinquencies, credit-loss allowances and net charge-offs. Liquidity could be constrained by market disruption, deposit outflows, higher commitment draws or loss of confidence; failure to meet capital requirements could limit buybacks, dividends or business activity. [S4]
- **Operational and cyber risks:** JPMorgan reports past system failures and disruptions, including degraded data processing, network interruptions, software malfunctions and third-party service interruptions, which have affected customers. It says cyber breaches have occurred and future breaches are inevitable, with potential consequences including service disruption, data loss, fraudulent transactions, litigation, penalties and reputational harm. [S4]

**Comparison:** Apple’s disclosed risks are closely tied to consumer demand, outsourced hardware production and platform regulation; Tesla’s to execution of ambitious product and manufacturing plans, component supply and product/financing risks; and JPMorgan’s to financial-market intermediation, regulated balance-sheet risks and operational resilience. [S1][S3][S4]

**Coverage:** The stated gap is: “Periods differ: the Companies' latest Filings here cover different periods (Apple: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-09-27; Tesla: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31; JPMorgan Chase: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31), so the comparison is not of the same period.” Apple’s Q1 FY2026 10-Q, report period 2025-12-27, says there were no material changes to its risk factors since the 2025 10-K. [S2] The supplied excerpts do not quantify the likelihood or financial impact of each risk or rank them by expected materiality.
items.fact: Apple says it is subject to antitrust investigations and litigation in various jurisdictions around the world.

Across the five pharmaceutical companies in scope, the regulatory risks the Sources name are drug-pricing controls, patent and exclusivity challenges, and FDA and manufacturing compliance. The Sources describe the risks far more than the company responses. Lilly's pricing arrangements with the U.S. government and AbbVie's patent defense are the clearest "addressing" examples [S2][S8].

**Companies in scope (from the Sector table):** Johnson & Johnson, Eli Lilly, Merck, Pfizer and AbbVie.

## Coverage Gaps
Periods differ: J&J (10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-28) and Lilly (10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31) are later than Merck, Pfizer and AbbVie (each 10-K FY2024, year to 2024-12-31), so the comparison is not of the same period.

## Johnson & Johnson (10-K FY2025)
- FDA delays: product approvals may be delayed by "limits on federal agency budgets or personnel, including reductions to the U.S. FDA's budget," which may lengthen review periods [S1].
- Patents: competitors challenge patents through litigation and inter partes review at the USPTO, and "at-risk" generic or biosimilar launches can cost a major portion of a product's revenue quickly [S1].
- Tax and trade: global minimum taxes, tariffs and other trade measures are cited [S1].
- Response: the Sources describe monitoring tax proposals and assessing audit outcomes to set reserves [S1]. They describe no regulatory-specific plan beyond that.

## Eli Lilly (10-K FY2025)
- Pricing: Lilly agreed with the U.S. government to lower Medicaid and certain other drug prices and to launch new medicines with a more balanced pricing approach across developed nations. It flags risks of delay, unfavorable terms, and revenue that may not offset pricing concessions [S2].
- Medicare: HHS selected Jardiance for government-set Medicare prices effective 2026 [S2].
- Counterfeit and compounded drugs: Lilly sees counterfeit, misbranded and mass-compounded incretins in the U.S. and says its actions to stop illegal sales are "costly and may be ineffective" [S2].
- Other: restrictions on direct-to-patient advertising, cGMP and nitrosamine scrutiny, and participation in the FDA Commissioner's National Priority Voucher Pilot Program [S2].
- Response: LillyDirect self-pay and new partnerships to expand access [S2].

## Merck (10-K FY2024)
- Pricing: Medicare and Medicaid laws, the ACA and the IRA, and state price-transparency laws [S3].
- Trade and China: the U.S. government announced plans to increase tariffs, and it is "too early" to assess the effect. Merck expects Gardasil/Gardasil 9 sales in China to decline significantly in 2025 [S3].
- Other: climate-related regulation and evolving privacy law, including in the EU and China [S3].
- Response: Merck self-insures substantially all product liability, having judged the available insurance not worth its cost [S3].

## Pfizer (10-K FY2024)
- Pricing: state prescription drug affordability boards, drug importation legislation, China's QCE and VBP tender process (significant price cuts for off-patent medicines), and the EU pharmaceutical reform proposal, which may alter exclusivity periods [S4]. The EU HTA-R took effect January 2025 [S4].
- Exclusivity: Pfizer anticipates a more significant revenue impact from expiries in 2026 through 2030 [S4].
- Safety: in September 2024 Pfizer voluntarily withdrew Oxbryta in all approved markets [S4].
- The 2025 10-Qs (Q1, Q2, Q3) only refer back to the 2024 10-K risk factors [S5][S6][S7].

## AbbVie (10-K FY2024)
- Patents: Abbreviated New Drug Applications, and inter partes and post grant review under the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act. Some governments may seek compulsory licenses [S8].
- Concentration: Humira, Skyrizi and Rinvoq were about 47% of 2024 net revenues, and Humira faces U.S. biosimilars after its 2023 loss of exclusivity [S8].
- Response: AbbVie "normally responds... by vigorously defending its patents, including by filing patent infringement lawsuits" [S8].

## Coverage
The gap above applies. The Sources give risk-factor text only, with no management plans for most regulatory risks, so "how they address them" is largely unanswered. No figures were drawn from a Financial Facts table.
items.fact: Pfizer says failure to comply with current Good Manufacturing Practices may subject it to warning letters, suspension of manufacturing or product recalls.

Meta’s revenue rose from **$164,501 million in FY2024** to **$200,966 million in FY2025**, a **derived 22.2% increase** year over year. The company attributed FY2025 growth to advertising revenue: advertising revenue increased **$35.54 billion, or 22%**, driven by higher ad impressions and average price per ad. [S4] [S8] [S14]

### Meta Platforms, Inc.

The comparison uses Meta’s 10-K filings for **FY2024 (report period December 31, 2024)** and **FY2025 (report period December 31, 2025)**. [S4] [S8]

| Fiscal period | Revenue |
|---|---:|
| FY2024, 12 months ended December 31, 2024 | $164,501 million [S4] |
| FY2025, 12 months ended December 31, 2025 | $200,966 million [S8] |

Meta reported FY2025 revenue growth of **22%** in its filing; the Financial Facts table gives the derived year-over-year rate as **+22.2%**. [S14] [S8] [S4]

**What drove the increase.** Advertising revenue was **$196,175 million** in FY2025, up **22%** from FY2024. Meta said the increase was due to more ad impressions and a higher average price per ad: impressions increased **12%**, while average price per ad increased **9%**. Impressions grew in all regions, especially Asia-Pacific, driven by increases in users and their engagement; Meta attributed the higher average price mainly to advertising demand, which it believed was mostly due to ongoing improvements to ad performance from its ad targeting and measurement tools. [S14]

The smaller revenue categories also grew, but from much lower bases. **Other revenue** increased **$862 million, or 50%**, mostly driven by paid messaging from WhatsApp and Meta Verified subscriptions. **Reality Labs revenue** increased **$61 million, or 3%**, as higher AI glasses sales were partially offset by lower Meta Quest sales. [S14]

The annual trend shows that revenue growth was not limited to FY2025: FY2024 revenue was **$164,501 million**, compared with **$134,902 million** in FY2023, and Meta reported a **22%** increase for FY2024 as well. Thus, reported annual growth was 22% in each of FY2024 and FY2025, while the Financial Facts table’s FY2025 growth calculation is 22.2%. [S4] [S8] [S14]

**Coverage:** There are no listed Coverage Gaps. This answer compares annual revenue and summarizes the FY2025 drivers disclosed in the filings; the cited materials do not provide a full driver breakdown for every quarter across the two years.
items.fact: Meta says its 2024 revenue increase was due to an increase in advertising revenue.

Microsoft’s revenue increased from **$245,122 million in FY2024** to **$281,724 million in FY2025**; the FY2025 10-K states that revenue rose **$36.6 billion, or 15%**, with growth across all three segments. The latest reported quarter in the supplied filings, Q2 FY2026, had revenue of **$81,273 million**, up **16.7%** from a year earlier. [S4] [S8] [S10] [S12]

### Microsoft

The comparison draws on Microsoft’s **10-Ks for FY2024 (report period June 30, 2024) and FY2025 (June 30, 2025)**, and **10-Qs for Q3 FY2024 (March 31, 2024), Q1–Q3 FY2025 (September 30, December 31, 2024, and March 31, 2025), and Q1–Q2 FY2026 (September 30 and December 31, 2025)**. [S3]–[S10]

| Fiscal period | Revenue |
|---|---:|
| FY2024 | $245,122 million [S4] |
| FY2025 | $281,724 million [S8] |
| Q3 FY2025 | $70,066 million; up 13.3% from a year earlier [S7] |
| Q4 FY2025 | $76,441 million, derived from FY2025 less Q1–Q3 FY2025; up 18.1% from a year earlier (derived) [S8] [S5] [S6] [S7] [S4] [S1] [S2] [S3] |
| Q1 FY2026 | $77,673 million; up 18.4% from a year earlier [S9] |
| Q2 FY2026 | $81,273 million; up 16.7% from a year earlier [S10] |

The FY2025 10-K attributes annual growth to **Intelligent Cloud, driven by Azure; Productivity and Business Processes, driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud; and More Personal Computing, driven by Gaming and Search and news advertising**. It reports Intelligent Cloud revenue of **$106,265 million**, up **21%**, and states that Azure and other cloud services revenue grew **34%**, driven by demand for Microsoft’s portfolio of services. Productivity and Business Processes revenue was **$120,810 million**; Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue grew **15%**, with seat growth of **6%** and growth in revenue per user. More Personal Computing revenue was **$54,649 million**, up **7%**. [S12] [S17]

The 10-Qs show strong year-over-year growth continuing into FY2026: revenue was **$77,673 million in Q1 FY2026** and **$81,273 million in Q2 FY2026**. In Q2, Microsoft Cloud revenue increased **26% to $51.5 billion**, while Azure and other cloud services revenue increased **39%**. [S10] [S14] In that quarter, overall revenue increased **$11.6 billion, or 17%**, driven by Intelligent Cloud and Productivity and Business Processes, partly offset by More Personal Computing. Microsoft also reported that cost of revenue rose **19%**, driven by Microsoft Cloud growth, and that Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to **67%**, citing continued AI infrastructure investment and growing AI product usage, partly offset by efficiency gains. [S14]

**Coverage:** There are no listed Coverage Gaps. The latest period covered is Q2 FY2026, reported December 31, 2025; the supplied filings do not provide later results.
items.fact: Microsoft says its fiscal year 2024 Intelligent Cloud revenue increase was driven by Azure.

NVIDIA’s reported revenue growth remained exceptionally strong, but its pace moderated from fiscal 2024 and through fiscal 2025; in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, year-over-year growth was still substantial, though it varied by quarter. **There is no company guidance in the Filings provided**: the outlook below is MD&A commentary and risk factors, not NVIDIA guidance. [S4] [S8] [S9] [S10] [S11]

### Revenue growth and the change in outlook

- **Fiscal 2024:** Revenue was **$60,922 million** for the 12 months ended January 28, 2024, up **126%** year over year, according to the 10-K MD&A. NVIDIA attributed the increase mainly to Data Center revenue, which was up **217%**, with demand from enterprise software and consumer internet applications and across industries including automotive, financial services, and healthcare. [S4] [S19]
- **Fiscal 2025:** Revenue was **$130,497 million** for the 12 months ended January 26, 2025, up **114.2%** year over year in the Financial Facts table; the 10-K MD&A described it as up **114%**. NVIDIA said fiscal-year growth was driven by Data Center compute and networking, with Hopper demand driving significant growth; production Blackwell systems began shipping in Q4. [S8] [S18]
- **Within fiscal 2025, growth decelerated quarter by quarter:** revenue growth was **262%** year over year in Q1, **122%** in Q2, and **94%** in Q3. The Q2 MD&A said it expected to ship “several billion dollars in Blackwell revenue” in Q4 FY2025, following a production ramp scheduled to begin in Q4. By Q3, NVIDIA said both Hopper and Blackwell systems had supply constraints and Blackwell demand was expected to exceed supply for several quarters in FY2026. These are successive MD&A statements, not formal guidance. [S17] [S15] [S16]
- **Fiscal 2026 through Q3:** Revenue was **$44,062 million** in Q1, **$46,743 million** in Q2, and **$57,006 million** in Q3; year-over-year growth was **69.2%**, **55.6%**, and **62.5%**, respectively. Thus growth remained high but was below the corresponding fiscal 2025 quarterly rates, with Q3 FY2026 growth higher than Q2. [S9] [S10] [S11]
- **What shaped the latest outlook commentary:** The April 2025 H20 export-license requirement for China and specified destinations led to a **$4.5 billion** charge for excess inventory and purchase obligations; NVIDIA said the requirements had impacted current revenue and would negatively affect future revenue. [S14] In Q2 FY2026, NVIDIA said Blackwell revenue ramp continued, including transition to Blackwell Ultra; in Q3, it said Blackwell architectures were the majority of Data Center revenue and Data Center growth was driven by accelerated computing, powerful AI models, and agentic applications. [S12] [S13]

### Coverage

Coverage includes NVIDIA 10-Ks for FY2024 and FY2025 and 10-Qs for Q1–Q3 FY2025 and Q1–Q3 FY2026; their report periods run from January 28, 2024 through October 26, 2025. **Coverage gap:** “No guidance in the Filings: NVIDIA's own guidance is not in the Filings provided; the outlook below is drawn from MD&A commentary and risk factors.” The excerpts do not establish management’s formal forward revenue targets beyond the cited commentary. [S4] [S5] [S6] [S7] [S8] [S9] [S10] [S11]
items.fact: NVIDIA said at the end of fiscal 2024 that it expected its next-generation products to be supply-constrained based on demand indications.

Tesla’s risk disclosures shifted from a broad emphasis on scaling vehicle and energy production, battery supply and EV demand in FY2024 to more explicit risks around autonomous services and Bots, dependence on Elon Musk, and the effects of 2025 trade-policy changes in FY2025. Many underlying risks persisted; the newer filings add specificity and describe some pressures—especially tariffs and incentives—as already affecting the business. [S4] [S2] [S3]

### How the risk emphasis changed

The comparison is between Tesla’s **10-K for FY2024, report period December 31, 2024**, and its **10-K for FY2025, report period December 31, 2025**. [S4] [S3]

| Risk area | FY2024 emphasis | FY2025 change or added detail |
|---|---|---|
| **Products and new businesses** | The FY2024 filing focused on launch and production-ramp delays, manufacturing costs and expanding mass-market vehicle output. It also identified challenges in developing AI products and services, including energy availability and data-center processing power. [S4] | The FY2025 filing makes autonomous driving and new product bets more prominent: it says Tesla launched its Robotaxi service in **June 2025**, plans mass production of **Cybercab**, and is developing **Bots, including Optimus**, without yet having commercialized them. It highlights uncertain consumer adoption, competition and the risk of launch or production delays. [S3] |
| **Leadership** | FY2024 warned that public criticism and speculation about management stability could undermine confidence, but the excerpt did not specifically identify the CEO as a key-person dependency. [S4] | FY2025 explicitly says Tesla is “highly dependent” on **Elon Musk**, notes that key employees are not bound by employment agreements for a specific term, and warns that losing key personnel could disrupt operations or delay products and services. [S3] |
| **Trade and incentives** | FY2024 described international trade restrictions, tariffs and uncertain foreign conditions as risks, and warned that changes to EV and energy incentives could hurt demand. [S4] | The FY2025 disclosures are more immediate: the 10-K says 2025 U.S. trade-policy changes—including heightened import tariffs and retaliatory measures—**have impacted supply-chain costs** and that tariff uncertainty has impacted product pricing. The Q2 FY2025 10-Q also identifies recent repeal or restriction of consumer, manufacturing and charging-infrastructure tax credits and regulatory-credit programs as potential demand and financial-result headwinds. [S3] [S2] |

### Risks that remained

Core operating exposures remained: dependence on a limited number of qualified battery-cell suppliers, including Panasonic and CATL; difficulty and investment requirements in developing Tesla’s own cells; and the risk that raw-material availability or prices constrain production or profitability. [S4] [S3] FY2024 also identified uncertain EV demand, competition and risks from product defects, regulatory scrutiny and international operations; the FY2025 filing continues to describe those types of exposures, including evolving product and regulatory risks. [S4] [S3]

**Coverage.** Coverage Gaps: **None.** The comparison uses the FY2024 and FY2025 10-Ks, with the Q2 FY2025 10-Q for the more specific incentive disclosure; the excerpts do not provide a quantified assessment of how much each risk changed or its financial impact.
items.fact: In its Q1 2025 10-Q, Tesla added a risk factor on U.S. trade policy changes, including significantly higher tariffs on imports.

UnitedHealth’s latest annual report—the **FY2024 Form 10-K, report period December 31, 2024**—describes cybersecurity risks involving attacks on its own systems and third-party vendors, exposure or misuse of sensitive information, and disruption to business operations. It says these events could cause financial loss, liability, regulatory consequences and reputational harm; the Q1, Q2 and Q3 FY2025 Forms 10-Q, for report periods March 31, June 30 and September 30, 2025, each state that there were no material changes to the 2024 10-K risk factors. [S1][S2][S3][S4]

### Cybersecurity risks described

- **Attacks and security incidents:** UnitedHealth says it is regularly targeted by attempted cyberattacks and other security threats, and has previously experienced compromises of its systems or information, including information held on its behalf by third parties. It specifically notes that its recently acquired Change Healthcare business was subject to a cyberattack in 2024 involving protected health information or personally identifiable information. [S1]

- **Evolving and hard-to-detect threats:** The company warns that techniques for unauthorized access, service disruption or sabotage change frequently and are becoming more sophisticated, in part through evolving AI/ML technologies, including generative AI. It may be unable to anticipate those techniques, detect incidents promptly or implement adequate preventive measures. [S1]

- **Operational disruption and compromised information:** Threat actors could penetrate security controls, disrupt or shut down systems and operations, or access, misappropriate or otherwise compromise protected personal information and proprietary or confidential information, including information belonging to third parties. The filing also identifies viruses, ransomware and other malware, as well as vulnerabilities in hardware, software or applications developed or procured from third parties. [S1]

- **Other paths to incidents:** The company identifies financial fraud schemes, misplaced or lost data, errors and malicious social engineering as risks to data, financial accounts and operations. It also says recently acquired or non-integrated businesses can create heightened vulnerabilities, and that third-party vendors processing, storing or transmitting data face similar risks outside UnitedHealth’s direct oversight and control. [S1]

- **Consequences and response:** A security incident could interrupt operations or services, lead to customer losses, increase remediation and operating costs, or expose the company to liability, litigation and regulatory penalties. Unauthorized disclosure could also result in financial or medical identity theft, misuse or loss of information, and damage to the company’s brand and reputation. UnitedHealth says it has detection, containment and response programs, employee security-awareness training, and business-continuation and resiliency plans that it maintains, updates and tests; it cautions that remediation may not succeed. [S1]

### Coverage

Coverage Gaps: **None.** The filings do not provide a separate, updated cybersecurity risk-factor discussion in the FY2025 quarterly reports; they state that there were no material changes to the FY2024 10-K risk factors. [S2][S3][S4]
items.fact: UnitedHealth says recently acquired or non-integrated businesses have brought heightened cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

Merck faces risks from drug-price controls, extensive product-approval and compliance requirements, and possible changes in U.S. health-care policy; it also identifies regulatory risks involving China, climate and sustainability reporting, and vaccine manufacturing. The provided filings do not include Bristol Myers Squibb, so I cannot assess its regulatory risks. [S1]

## Merck & Co Inc (MRK)

**Filing basis:** 10-K, FY2024, report period December 31, 2024. [S1]

- **Drug pricing and reimbursement:** Merck says U.S. pricing pressure includes Medicare and Medicaid laws and regulations, the Affordable Care Act (ACA), the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), managed-care and institutional purchasers, and state price-transparency laws. The IRA provides for inflation-related penalties, greater manufacturer liability under Medicare Part D from 2025, and government price setting for certain Part D drugs beginning in 2026 and Part B drugs beginning in 2028. HHS selected Januvia for a government-set price effective January 1, 2026, and Janumet and Janumet XR for one effective January 1, 2027; Merck expects Keytruda to be selected in 2026 for a price effective January 1, 2028. [S1]
- **Other U.S. payment and policy changes:** Merck identifies the removal, beginning in January 2024, of the statutory cap on manufacturer rebates to Medicaid as a risk, including the possibility that rebates exceed the Average Manufacturer Price for some products. It also says increased use of the 340B Federal Drug Discount Program, limits on identifying inappropriate discounts, and state Prescription Drug Affordability Boards’ potential upper payment limits may negatively affect performance. Potential changes to HHS, FDA and CDC policies could affect drug and vaccine approvals or vaccine recommendations; eliminating FDA user-fee programs could delay inspections and approvals. [S1]
- **Approvals and ongoing oversight:** Merck’s research, trials, manufacturing and marketing are subject to extensive U.S. and foreign regulation, including by the FDA and authorities in the EU, Japan and China. Authorities can require additional testing, delay or withhold approvals, or prevent distribution; Merck cannot market products without required approvals and must maintain them. Post-approval trial results, safety reviews, recalls, labeling changes, advertising scrutiny, or withdrawal of accelerated-approval indications can also reduce demand or sales. [S1]
- **China and manufacturing:** Merck says China’s anti-corruption campaign, including increased inspections and audits, could increase administrative burdens on health-care institutions and professionals and potentially hurt sales. It also reports manufacturing delays for Varivax and ProQuad that will constrain supply in 2025, and identifies compliance with Current Good Manufacturing Practices and other regulations as a risk because failures could cause shutdowns, shortages or delays. [S1]
- **Other laws and reporting:** Merck lists evolving U.S. and international requirements covering data privacy, local manufacturing, reporting payments to health-care professionals, sustainability, import restrictions, embargoes and trade sanctions. It specifically cites the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, California GHG-emissions and climate-risk reporting legislation, and potentially SEC climate-related reporting requirements, which it says are currently stayed. [S1]

## Bristol Myers Squibb

The provided materials contain no Bristol Myers Squibb filing, so its regulatory risks cannot be assessed here.

## Coverage

The only filing provided is Merck’s 10-K for FY2024, report period December 31, 2024; Merck is a snapshot company with one filing. **Not in the Corpus:** Bristol Myers Squibb is not in the Filings provided, so this answer does not cover it. The Sources therefore cannot support a comparison with Bristol Myers Squibb or describe its regulatory risks.
items.fact: Merck expects U.S. sales of Keytruda to decline beginning in January 2028 when government pricing under the Inflation Reduction Act takes effect.

Apple's disclosed risks center on its outsourced, Asia-concentrated supply chain, U.S. Tariffs and trade measures, and regulation such as the EU Digital Markets Act [S1]. Tesla's center on executing new products (Cybercab, Optimus Bots, AI), supplier and tariff exposure, and dependence on Elon Musk [S3]. JPMorgan's are those of a regulated bank: supervision, credit, liquidity, capital, cyber and operational risks [S4]. Apple and Tesla share supply-chain, tariff and FX exposures, while JPMorgan's risks are balance-sheet and regulatory. The Companies' latest Filings cover different periods (Apple: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-09-27; Tesla: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31; JPMorgan Chase: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31), so the comparison is not of the same period.

## Apple (10-K FY2025, period ended 2025-09-27; 10-Q Q1 FY2026, period ended 2025-12-27)
- **Supply chain:** A significant majority of manufacturing is done by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Apple relies on single-source partners and on Asian partners for final assembly of substantially all hardware [S1].
- **Trade:** U.S. Tariffs were announced beginning in Q2 2025 on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU. Countries have responded with reciprocal tariffs. The Department of Commerce has opened a Section 232 investigation into semiconductors and downstream products [S1].
- **Regulation:**
  - Apple has made DMA compliance changes in the EU, including alternative fee structures, distribution and payment processing. The Commission has challenged the compliance plan [S1].
  - In the U.S., a court order bars any commission or fee on certain App Store purchases [S1].
- **Financial:**
  - Gross margins face pressure from pricing, components, tariffs and FX [S1].
  - A significant portion of net sales comes from a single product category [S1].
  - Vendor non-trade receivables are concentrated among a few vendors in Asia [S1].
  - Apple faces tax exposure in jurisdictions including Ireland and Singapore [S1].
- **Q1 FY2026 update:** The 10-Q reports no material changes to these risk factors [S2].

## Tesla (10-K FY2025, period ended 2025-12-31)
- **Execution:**
  - The future business depends on driver assistance and autonomy, and on ramping mass-market vehicles including Cybercab, its purpose-built Robotaxi [S3].
  - Optimus Bots are not yet commercialized [S3].
  - AI work faces energy, processing-power and data-center power constraints [S3].
- **Suppliers:** Tesla buys thousands of parts from hundreds of suppliers, including single-source suppliers. U.S. trade policy alterations in 2025 have impacted supply chain costs [S3].
- **Key person:** Tesla is highly dependent on Elon Musk. It also flags a risk that the 2025 CEO Performance Award's product goals are misaligned with demand [S3].
- **Financing:** Leasing creates residual value risk, residual value guarantees and customer credit risk [S3].
- **Debt:** Tesla had $8.18 billion of indebtedness as of December 31, 2025 (read from the Filing text) [S3].
- **Other:**
  - Product liability for vehicles is largely self-insured [S3].
  - Lithium-ion cells carry fire risk [S3].
  - Government investigations are ongoing, involving the SEC and DOJ [S3].
  - The stock traded between $214.25 and $498.83 over the last 52 weeks [S3].

## JPMorgan Chase (10-K FY2025, period ended 2025-12-31)
- **Legal/Regulatory:** The Firm is subject to extensive supervision. It may face stricter rules than fintech competitors and executive branch actions [S4].
- **Credit:**
  - Exposure to counterparties and central counterparties (CCPs), including sharing in member and non-default losses [S4].
  - Consumer credit is sensitive to unemployment and student loans [S4].
  - The expansion of private credit could worsen losses among non-bank lenders [S4].
- **Liquidity and capital:**
  - Liquidity could be hit by Federal Reserve balance sheet reduction and deposit loss [S4].
  - Credit rating downgrades could raise funding costs [S4].
  - CCAR stress losses could raise the stress capital buffer (SCB), limiting buybacks and dividends [S4].
- **Operational:**
  - The Firm has experienced breaches and says future breaches are "inevitable" [S4].
  - AI and quantum computing threats may require quantum-resistant encryption [S4].
  - Competitors may deploy AI faster, and AI agents could disintermediate customer relationships [S4].
- **Climate:** Both physical and transition risks apply [S4].

## Comparison

|---|---|---|---|
| Core exposure | Outsourced Asian manufacturing [S1] | New-product ramps, autonomy, Bots [S3] | Credit, liquidity, capital [S4] |

| AI | Safety and IP issues [S1] | Core to strategy [S3] | Cyber threat and competitive risk [S4] |
| Cyber | High-profile target [S1] | Vehicle hacking, vendor ransomware [S3] | Breaches "inevitable" [S4] |

## Coverage
- **Coverage Gap:** Periods differ: the Companies' latest Filings cover different periods (Apple: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-09-27; Tesla: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31; JPMorgan Chase: 10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31), so the comparison is not of the same period.

Apple's risk factors center on tariffs, a China/Asia-concentrated supply chain and EU/US App Store regulation [S1]. Tesla's center on ramping new products (Cybercab, Bots), supplier and battery risks, and dependence on Elon Musk [S3]. JPMorgan's are mainly regulatory, credit, liquidity, capital and cyber risks [S4]. The periods differ: Apple's 10-K is for the year to 2025-09-27, while Tesla's and JPMorgan's 10-Ks are for the year to 2025-12-31, so the comparison is not of the same period.

## Apple (10-K FY2025, year to 2025-09-27)
- **Trade and tariffs:** Beginning in Q2 2025, new U.S. Tariffs were announced, including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU. A Section 232 investigation covers semiconductors. The Filing says the ultimate impact remains uncertain [S1].
- **Supply chain:** A significant majority of manufacturing is done by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Single-source partners supply many components [S1].
- **Regulation:** Apple is subject to a court order barring it from imposing any commission or fee on certain U.S. App Store purchases. It has changed iOS, the App Store and Safari in the EU to comply with the Digital Markets Act. The Commission has challenged that plan, and the DMA provides for significant fines [S1].
- **Financial:** Gross margins face downward pressure, and a significant portion of net sales comes from a single product category. Apple also cites foreign exchange exposure and unsecured vendor non-trade receivables concentrated among a few vendors in Asia [S1].
- **Latest update:** The Q1 FY2026 10-Q (period 2025-12-27) reports no material changes to the risk factors [S2].

## Tesla (10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31)
- **Execution:** The future business depends on driver assistance, autonomous driving, and mass-market vehicles including Cybercab, the purpose-built Robotaxi. Tesla also cites production ramp delays and the energy and processing demands of its data centers [S3].
- **Bots:** Optimus is in a nascent industry that has not yet commercialized [S3].
- **Suppliers and trade:** Tesla buys parts from hundreds of suppliers, including single-source ones. U.S. trade policy changes in 2025, including heightened tariffs, have impacted supply chain costs [S3].
- **Operations and product:** Lithium-ion cell production at its Gigafactories is a risk, as are battery fires. Tesla generally self-insures vehicle product liability [S3].
- **Key person and financing:** The Filing states a high dependence on Elon Musk. Indebtedness was $8.18 billion at December 31, 2025. Residual value guarantees and leasing add further exposure [S3].
- **Stock:** The 52-week range was $214.25 to $498.83, and the Filing flags possible misalignment with the 2025 CEO Performance Award goals [S3].

## JPMorgan Chase (10-K FY2025, year to 2025-12-31)
- **Regulation:** The firm is highly regulated and could be forced to limit products, raise prices or dispose of assets. Executive orders can also affect it, and fintech competitors may face less stringent oversight [S4].
- **Credit and market:** Counterparty and CCP defaults are named risks. The Filing also flags private credit expansion and consumer credit stress, such as student loans, which could raise charge-offs [S4].
- **Liquidity and capital:** Credit rating downgrades could raise funding costs. Capital shortfalls, including a higher stress capital buffer (SCB) from CCAR, could limit buybacks and dividends [S4].
- **Operational:** The firm says cyber breaches are "inevitable" and cites AI and quantum computing as intensifiers. It also flags AI competitive disadvantage and climate change [S4].

## Comparison
| Theme | Apple | Tesla | JPMorgan |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trade/tariffs | Central [S1] | Supply costs affected [S3] | Market-risk factor [S4] |
| Regulation | DMA, App Store order [S1] | Investigations, direct-sales limits [S3] | Core, bank supervision [S4] |
| Tech/AI | AI features add safety and IP risk [S1] | AI and autonomy are the growth bet [S3] | AI competition and cyber [S4] |
| Balance-sheet | FX, receivables [S1] | Debt, residual values [S3] | Liquidity, capital, credit [S4] |

## Coverage
Gap: periods differ (Apple year to 2025-09-27; Tesla and JPMorgan year to 2025-12-31). The Sources are risk-factor excerpts only. They give no financial figures and no guidance, so the risks cannot be ranked by size or likelihood.
